On a conceptual level this looks like our futex API.

You have a wait API, and then two APIs: one that wakes one, and one that wakes all. Futex is the same, except the wake function has a boolean for wake one / wake all, and we sync on a mutex instead of an atomic variable
monitor objects could be added along with these condition variables (in another commit), at least it would make user's life simpler for instance on suspend/resume sample.

issue_context.title: Condition variables
issue_context.body:
Zephyr kernel APIs that cover:

```
pthread_cond_wait
pthread_cond_timedwait
pthread_cond_signal
pthread_cond_broadcast
```
comments:
Draft API for condition variables...

```
/**
 * @brief Initialize a condition variable
 *
 * @param condvar pointer to a @p k_condvar structure
 * @retval 0 Condition variable created successfully
 */
__syscall int k_condvar_init(struct k_condvar *condvar);

/**
 * @brief Signals one thread that is pending on the condition variable
 *
 *
 * @param condvar pointer to a @p k_condvar structure
 * @retval 0 On success
 */
__syscall int k_condvar_signal(struct k_condvar *condvar);

/**
 * @brief Broadcast to all threads that are pending on the condition variable
 *
 * @param condvar pointer to a @p k_condvar structure
 * @retval 0 On success
 */
__syscall int k_condvar_broadcast(struct k_condvar *condvar);

/**
 * @brief Waits on the condition variable releasing the mutex lock
 *
 * Automically releases the currently owned mutex, blocks the current thread
 * waiting on the condition variable specified by @a condvar,
 * and finally acquires the mutex again.
 *
 * The waiting thread unblocks only after another thread calls k_condvar_signal, or
 * k_condvar_broadcast with the same condition variable.
 *
 * @param condvar pointer to a @p k_condvar structure
 * @param mutex Address of the mutex.
 * @param timeout Waiting period for the condition variable in ms
 *                or one of the special values K_NO_WAIT and K_FOREVER.
 * @return
 */
__syscall int k_condvar_wait(struct k_condvar *condvar, struct k_mutex *mutex,
			     k_timeout_t timeout);

/**
 * @brief Statically define and initialize a condition variable.
 *
 * The condition variable can be accessed outside the module where it is defined using:
 *
 * @code extern struct k_condvar <name>; @endcode
 *
 * @param name Name of the condition variable.
 */
#define K_CONDVAR_DEFINE(name)                                                 \
	Z_STRUCT_SECTION_ITERABLE(k_condvar, name) =                           \
		Z_CONDVAR_INITIALIZER(name);

```

review_comments: Same issue here, the return value needs to be specified better in the documentation.
Yes: this is exactly why "non-negative is success" is so useful: to return the number of things affected.
The posix counterparts return only 0 for success and <0 for error. Do we really need to know the count here?
It's useful in testing, since there's no other indicator that something did or did not happen.  But if we're striving to match an existing API, maybe it's not right to do that.

If we have in the future `pthread_cond_xxx()` API which returns <0 on error and 0 on success, then it should be quite trivial to check that if `k_condvar_signal/broadcast()` returns >= 0, then return 0 in the pthread variant. So the zephyr API does not need to match exactly to pthread one in this case.
Coverage shows none of these are being invoked.
Confirmed; possibly this was at a point were I didn't realize there were multiple tests so focused the -T argument too tightly.

The standard semantics of condition variables requires that the unlock, queue, and wait be done atomically.  This code leaves a gap where the signal could be sent before the thread is queued to receive it, causing a failure.

You'd need to move the spin lock before the mutex unlock to avoid that.
Should we also document that all values !=0 are error, or just <0 is error? The documentation is ambiguous here
I like negative is error, non-negative is success, but agree that potential error returns should be documented.  As is the natural question is "if it can only return 0, why isn't it `void`?"

As a general note, I would argue that even if the function does not return <0, it might in the future if more error checks or conditions are added. In that case it would make sense to return int, even if we always return >= 0. It is difficult to change the API afterwards.
